How do pest control companies get more customers?

8 min read

Pest control is one of the few trades built on recurring revenue, so the goal isn't just more calls — it's more customers who sign quarterly or annual plans. The companies that grow win the urgent one-off caller fast, then convert them into long-term contracts, while ranking for seasonal pest searches and stacking reviews that prove they actually solve the problem. Treat lifetime value, not the first invoice, as the prize.

Most trades sell a job. Pest control sells a relationship — and that changes everything about how you should market. A plumber fixes the leak and may never hear from that customer again. You treat the ant problem in May, the wasps in July, the rodents in October, and if you do it right, that household pays you every quarter for the next ten years. The recurring contract is the entire business model, and the company that understands its true lifetime value will out-market the one chasing one-off sprays every time.

Win the urgent caller, then convert them

Almost every pest control customer starts the same way: something is wrong right now. Roaches in the kitchen, a wasp nest by the door, mice in the walls. They're not patient and they're not loyal yet — they're typing "exterminator near me" or "how to get rid of [pest]" into Google and calling the first credible company that answers.

So step one is being the company that answers. Pest calls spike seasonally and unpredictably, and a missed call is a customer who phones the next listing. Worse, in pest control a missed call isn't just a lost $250 treatment — it's a lost multi-year recurring contract. The math on a missed call is brutal when you count lifetime value. We lay it out in what missed calls are costing your business, and an AI receptionist can capture and book the after-hours and overflow callers you're losing today.

Then comes the move that separates growing companies from stagnant ones: turn the one-off into a plan. The roach treatment isn't the sale — it's the audition. Train every tech and CSR to offer the quarterly program at the moment the customer is most relieved and most convinced you're competent.

Rank for the seasonal pest calendar

Pests run on a calendar, and so should your marketing. Ants and termites swarm in spring, mosquitoes and wasps own the summer, rodents move indoors in fall, and overwintering pests show up when it cools. Each one is a wave of searches you can either catch or miss.

  • Build seasonal content and service pages for the pests in your region — "termite swarm season in [city]," "fall rodent prevention." These answer the exact questions homeowners Google right before they call.
  • Time promotions to the wave: a mosquito-program push as the weather warms, a rodent-exclusion offer in early fall.
  • Own the map pack for "exterminator near me" year-round, since the top three results take about 44% of clicks. Start with our Google Business Profile optimization guide.

Reviews prove the problem stays gone

Here's what a pest control customer is actually afraid of: paying you, and then the bugs come back. 97% of consumers read reviews before hiring, and for pest control they're scanning for proof of results — "haven't seen a roach since," "finally got rid of the ants for good." Reviews that mention the problem being permanently solved are worth more than any ad. And because recurring customers interact with you four times a year, you have four natural moments to ask. Our guide to getting more Google reviews shows how to make asking automatic.

Your existing customers are a renewal machine

The cheapest growth in pest control isn't new customers — it's keeping and expanding the ones you have. A household on a quarterly plan can be upsold to termite monitoring, mosquito service, or a wildlife program. A simple, consistent email and text rhythm — service reminders, seasonal tips, renewal nudges — keeps churn down and revenue compounding. Past-customer marketing is repeatedly cited as the single best lead source in the trades, and in a recurring-revenue business it's even more powerful. See how it stacks up in the best lead sources for contractors.

Skip the shared-lead trap

Pest control companies get aggressively pitched by lead platforms, but think about what you're buying: a single urgent caller, sold simultaneously to three to five competitors, at a price that ignores the fact you're trying to win a recurring contract, not a one-time job. You end up in a race-to-the-bottom price war for a relationship business. Build your own pipeline instead — here's how to get off HomeAdvisor and Angi and own your leads.

Don't forget commercial accounts

Residential plans are steady, but commercial contracts — restaurants, warehouses, property managers, apartment complexes — are the whales of pest control. They sign recurring agreements, they renew for years, and they refer other businesses. A handful of these accounts can stabilize your whole revenue base. Marketing to them is different: it leans on referrals, local reputation, and a website that signals you can handle commercial compliance and scheduling. If you're wondering whether the site even matters, we settle it in do contractors need a website in 2026.

The throughline across all of this is simple: stop optimizing for the first invoice. A pest control customer is worth ten times more over their lifetime than the treatment that got them in the door. Market for the relationship, and the growth takes care of itself.

Frequently asked questions

How do pest control companies get more recurring customers?

Win the urgent one-off caller first, then convert them to a quarterly or annual plan at the moment they are most relieved and most convinced you are competent. Train every tech and CSR to offer the program, because the recurring contract, not the first treatment, is where the real lifetime value lives.

What marketing works best for pest control?

Rank in Google's map pack for 'exterminator near me' year-round, build seasonal content around the pests in your region, stack reviews that prove the problem stays gone, and market consistently to your existing plan customers. Together these capture the urgent caller and maximize lifetime value.

How important are reviews for pest control companies?

Very. With 97% of consumers reading reviews before hiring, and pest customers specifically afraid the bugs will come back, reviews that mention the problem being permanently solved do powerful selling. Recurring customers also give you four natural moments a year to ask.

Should pest control companies go after commercial accounts?

Yes. Commercial contracts with restaurants, warehouses, and property managers are the highest-value accounts in pest control, since they sign multi-year recurring agreements and refer other businesses. Winning them leans on referrals, local reputation, and a website that signals you can handle commercial scheduling and compliance.
